title: WHY DID GOD LEAD YOU INTO THE VALLEY WHEN HE COULD HAVE TAKEN YOU AROUND IT?
paragraphs:
WHY DID GOD LEAD YOU INTO THE VALLEY WHEN HE COULD HAVE TAKEN YOU AROUND IT?
Understanding Psalm 23:4 — The Shepherd Who Does Not Always Remove the Valley, but Refuses to Let the Valley Have You
There is one word in Psalm 23 that many hurting Christians read too quickly.
Through.
Not around.
Not away from.
Not untouched by.
Through.
And maybe that word bothers you more than you would ever admit in church.
Because if God is really your Shepherd, why did He allow the diagnosis?
Why did He let the person you prayed for walk away?
Why did He allow the betrayal to happen?
Why didn't He stop the door from closing?
Why did you lose something you begged Him to save?
Why did He remain silent when you were crying so hard you could barely form a prayer?
You know the verses.
You know the worship songs.
You know Christians are supposed to say, “God is good.”
But somewhere beneath the practiced smile is a question you have been afraid to say aloud:
“If You are really leading me, Lord… why am I here?”
And Psalm 23 gives an answer that is far more powerful than the shallow promise that following God means avoiding painful places.
David writes:
The Hebrew is hauntingly beautiful:
גַּם כִּי־אֵלֵךְ בְּגֵיא צַלְמָוֶת לֹא־אִירָא רָע כִּי־אַתָּה עִמָּדִי
Gam ki-elekh begei tsalmavet, lo-ira ra, ki-attah immadi.
A careful rendering is:
“Even though I walk through a valley of deep darkness, I will fear no evil, because You are with me.”
That phrase traditionally translated “the shadow of death” comes from the Hebrew צַלְמָוֶת — tsalmavet.
It can carry the sense of death-shadow, deep darkness, or deathly gloom. The image is not merely of someone having a disappointing afternoon.
This is darkness.
Threat.
Vulnerability.
The kind of place where you cannot clearly see what is ahead.
And notice what David does not say.
He does not say:
“God would never allow me into a valley.”
He says:
“Though I walk through…”
That changes everything.
Because Psalm 23 begins with a Shepherd.
“The LORD is my shepherd…”
The Hebrew word translated “shepherd” comes from רָעָה — ra'ah, carrying the idea of tending, pasturing, feeding, shepherding.
David knew shepherding personally.
And the shocking movement of Psalm 23 is that the same Shepherd associated with green pastures and still waters is still present when the scenery becomes frightening.
The Shepherd has not changed because the landscape has changed.
Read that again.
The Shepherd has not changed because the landscape has changed.
Somebody needs that tonight.
Because you have been interpreting the valley as evidence that God abandoned you.
You have been looking at the darkness and concluding that the Shepherd must have disappeared.
But Psalm 23 refuses that conclusion.
The green pasture has a Shepherd.
The still water has a Shepherd.
And the valley has the same Shepherd.
Christian faith never promises that belonging to God means never suffering.
Jesus certainly never promised that.
He told His disciples plainly:
“In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world.” — John 16:33
Jesus did not sell His followers a painless Christianity.
The Gospel is not, “Come to Jesus and nothing terrible will ever happen again.”

The Gospel is that sinners can be reconciled to God through the crucified and risen Christ—and that nothing, not even suffering or death, can ultimately separate those who belong to Christ from the love of God.
Sometimes God delivers us from suffering.
Sometimes God sustains us through suffering.
And Scripture does not give us permission to pretend we always know exactly why God permits a particular valley.
That matters.
We should be careful about telling grieving people, “God did this because He wanted to teach you something.”
We do not know every hidden purpose of God.
Job's friends made the mistake of confidently explaining suffering they did not understand.
Sometimes the most biblical response to another person's valley is not an explanation.
Sometimes it is simply sitting beside them and refusing to leave.
But Scripture does reveal something extraordinary:
God can accomplish purposes in suffering that suffering itself could never accomplish.
Joseph was betrayed by his brothers, sold, falsely accused, imprisoned, and forgotten.
Years later he could say:
“But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good…” — Genesis 50:20
Notice carefully.
Joseph did not call evil good.
He called it evil.
But evil did not get the final sentence.
God did.
That distinction is essential.
Christianity does not require you to call abuse good.
It does not require you to call betrayal good.
It does not require you to call cancer good.
It does not require you to call death good.
Death itself is described in Scripture as an enemy.
But Christianity makes an astonishing claim:
evil is never sovereign. God is.
And the God who rules over history is so sovereign that even what human beings intend for destruction cannot finally overthrow His redemptive purposes.
That is why Romans 8:28 does not mean everything that happens to you is good.
It means God works in all things for the good of those who love Him and are called according to His purpose.
There is a difference.
And maybe that is where your valley begins to make sense.
Not completely.
Maybe not yet.
But enough to keep walking.
Because David doesn't say:
“Though I understand the valley…”
He says:
“Though I walk through the valley…”
Faith sometimes walks before understanding arrives.
One foot.
Then another.
One prayer.
Then another.
One morning when you did not think you could get out of bed.
One worship song sung through tears.
One whispered, “Jesus, help me.”
One more day choosing not to surrender your soul to despair.
That is still faith.
Maybe nobody applauded you.
Maybe nobody knew how close you came to giving up.
But heaven saw you keep walking.
And there is another detail in Psalm 23 that is easy to miss.
Before verse 4, David speaks about God.
“He maketh me…”
“He leadeth me…”
“He restoreth my soul…”
Then the valley appears.
And suddenly David speaks to God.
“For THOU art with me.”
The grammar becomes intimate.
The valley changes the conversation.
In the pasture, David talks about the Shepherd.
In the darkness, David talks to Him.
There are things you can learn about God in comfortable seasons.
But suffering often strips Christianity of borrowed language.
Eventually somebody else's testimony is not enough.
Your mother's faith cannot carry you forever.
Your pastor's relationship with Jesus cannot substitute for yours.
Your favorite preacher cannot pray every midnight prayer for you.
At some point, somewhere in the darkness, Christianity becomes painfully personal.
“You are with me.”
Not merely:
“God was with Moses.”
Not merely:
“God was with David.”
Not merely:
“God was with Paul.”
But:
“Jesus… are You here with me?”
And the Gospel answers with something greater than sentimental reassurance.
Look at the cross.
Christianity does not worship a God who remained safely distant from human suffering.
Jesus entered it.
He was betrayed.
Rejected.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Humiliated.
Crucified.
He knew anguish.
He knew abandonment by friends.
He knew what it was to face death.
And at Calvary, the sinless Son of God bore our sins.
Isaiah had prophesied:
“But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities…” — Isaiah 53:5
Peter later writes that Christ:
The deepest human problem is not that our lives sometimes become painful.
Our deepest problem is sin.
We have sinned against a holy God.
No amount of positive thinking can remove guilt.
No amount of religious performance can purchase forgiveness.
No valley experience makes us righteous.
We need a Savior.
And that Savior is Jesus Christ.
He died for sinners.
He was buried.
He rose again.
And through repentance and faith in Him, sinners receive forgiveness, reconciliation, and eternal life—not because we finally became good enough, but because Christ is enough.
This is where Psalm 23 becomes bigger than motivational encouragement.
The Shepherd David trusted ultimately points our eyes toward Christ, who identifies Himself as:
“the good shepherd.” — John 10:11
And Jesus says something breathtaking:
“The good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.”
The Shepherd entered death for His sheep.
And He came out alive.
So when a Christian walks through the valley of death's shadow, we follow a Shepherd who has already walked into death and defeated it through His resurrection.
That does not mean Christians do not grieve.
We do.
Sometimes terribly.
It does not mean we never feel afraid.
It does not mean depression instantly disappears, relationships instantly heal, bills mysteriously vanish, or every disease is cured.
Psalm 23 does not promise that.
It promises something deeper:
“You are with me.”
Sometimes the miracle is the door opening.
Sometimes the miracle is discovering Christ is enough when the door stays closed.
Sometimes God calms the storm.
Sometimes He carries His child through it.
Sometimes He changes the circumstance.
Sometimes, while we plead for Him to change the circumstance, He begins changing us.
And perhaps you are reading this from inside a valley right now.
Nobody knows.
Your Facebook photos look normal.
Your family thinks you are fine.
You still answer messages.
You still laugh occasionally.
You still say, “I'm okay.”
But at night…
when everyone disappears…
something inside you aches.
Maybe you lost someone.
Maybe your marriage feels like it is slowly dying.
Maybe your child is far from God.
Maybe you fell back into the sin you swore you would never touch again.
Maybe you have been secretly questioning your faith.
Maybe you are exhausted from being “the strong Christian.”
Maybe you are carrying shame over something nobody knows.
Maybe your greatest fear isn't that God cannot forgive you.
Maybe your fear is that if people discovered what you have done, they wouldn't.
Listen carefully.
There was scandal at the cross.
A holy Christ crucified between criminals.
The innocent condemned.
The guilty offered mercy.
A dying thief with nothing left to offer Christ except faith.
No lifetime left to repair his reputation.
No ministry résumé.
No religious performance.
No opportunity to prove himself.
Only:
“Lord, remember me…” — Luke 23:42
And Jesus gave him hope.
That is grace.
Grace does not pretend sin doesn't matter.
Grace cost Jesus blood.
Grace does not excuse rebellion.
Grace calls sinners to repentance.
But grace also means your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Peter denied Jesus.
Thomas doubted.
Paul persecuted Christians.
The prodigal wasted what his father gave him.
David himself knew devastating moral failure.
Scripture does not sanitize these stories.
And Scripture does not tell them so we can romanticize sin.
It tells them so we can see the astonishing mercy of a God who restores repentant sinners.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling sin righteousness.
Not by erasing consequences with religious slogans.
Jesus rewrites everything by forgiving sinners, restoring the broken, giving new hearts, transforming lives, and making people who were once dead in sin alive in Him.
Maybe the valley has finally exposed something you successfully hid in the pasture.
Maybe you were depending on money.
Approval.
A relationship.
Your appearance.
Your ministry reputation.
Pornography.
Alcohol.
Achievement.
Control.
Your ability to keep everybody impressed.
And then the valley stripped your hands empty.
You thought emptiness meant God had abandoned you.
But what if the empty hands are finally able to reach for Christ?
Not because every valley is sent as punishment.
Scripture does not teach that.
But God can use suffering to expose what comfort allowed us to conceal.
David says:
“Thy rod and thy staff they comfort me.”
The Shepherd's instruments communicate protection, direction, and care.
And there is something beautiful about biblical comfort:
comfort is not always God explaining everything.
Sometimes comfort is God's presence when explanations would not be enough anyway.
You keep asking:
“Why?”
And perhaps someday God will allow you to understand pieces of it.
Perhaps some answers will remain beyond you in this life.
But Psalm 23 gives you something to hold while the unanswered questions remain:
כִּי־אַתָּה עִמָּדִי — ki-attah immadi.
“For You are with me.”
That might be the sentence you need to whisper tonight.
Not because you feel it.
Because He has promised His presence.
You are with me.
When the test result comes.
You are with me.
When the person leaves.
You are with me.
When repentance hurts.
You are with me.
When temptation returns.
You are with me.
When the funeral ends and everybody else goes home.
You are with me.
When nobody understands.
You are with me.
When I cannot understand myself.
You are with me.
And notice the destination.
Psalm 23 does not end in the valley.
“Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life: and I will dwell in the house of the LORD for ever.”
The valley is real.
But it is not home.
For everyone who belongs to Jesus Christ, darkness does not receive the final word.
Death does not receive the final word.
Your failure does not receive the final word.
Your enemies do not receive the final word.
Your past does not receive the final word.
Jesus does.
And maybe the question is no longer simply:
“Why did God allow this valley?”
Maybe another question is forming:
“Who am I becoming while I walk through it with Him?”
If your valley has exposed sin, repent.
Don't hide.
Don't rename it.
Don't defend it.
Bring it into the light before Christ.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9
If your valley has exposed exhaustion, stop pretending strength you do not possess.
If your valley has exposed fear, bring that fear to the Shepherd.
If you have wandered from Jesus, come home.
If you have never truly trusted Christ, do not mistake Christian content for Christianity.
Reading articles about Jesus cannot save you.
Following Christian pages cannot save you.
Buying Christian products cannot save you.
Giving money to ministry cannot save you.
Jesus saves.
Turn from sin.
Trust Him.
Come to Christ.
Be honest.
You do not have to publish every private detail of your pain. But there is something powerful about refusing to let shame convince you that you must fight alone.
And if Christ has already carried you through a valley you once believed would destroy you, tell somebody what He did.
Your testimony may become another person's reason to keep walking tonight.
Not as a superstition.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God.
It doesn't.
“Someone I know needs this.”
Send it privately if that would be kinder.
Come back when the darkness gets loud.

If you genuinely want to glorify God through the resources He has entrusted to you, prayerfully consider whether supporting Gospel work is one way He is calling you to do that. Scripture teaches cheerful, willing generosity—not manipulated giving.
And there is more waiting for people who are serious about growing deeper in Christ.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend quietly drifting from God.
Invite the believer who is exhausted.
Invite the skeptic who thinks Christianity has nothing to say about suffering.
Invite the person who has fallen and believes God could never want them again.
But before you leave, remember the word we started with.
Through.
You may be in the valley.
You may hate the valley.
You may not understand the valley.
You may still be crying in the valley.
But if you belong to Christ, the valley does not own you.
The darkness does not get to name you.
Your failure does not get to define you.
And death itself does not get to keep you.
The Shepherd is still leading.
The Shepherd is still present.
The Shepherd still knows your name.
And because Jesus Christ died and rose again, those who belong to Him are walking toward a Kingdom where the shadows finally end.
So keep walking.
Even slowly.
Even trembling.
Even with tears running down your face.
The valley may change the sound of your voice, but it cannot silence the Shepherd who is calling you home.
